subject: Re: Redwood vs Hyperscaler inference — post-demo follow-up and next tests
messages:
From: Tom Reynolds <tom.reynolds@datacloud.io>
To: aditya_rao <aditya@redwood.ai>
Date: 2026-02-10T09:12:00-05:00
Subject: Redwood demo — follow-up questions

Thanks for the demo this morning, Aditya. A few quick items from our side as we think about next steps: 

- Can you confirm how Redwood compares to the hyperscalers on latency for small- to medium-sized prompts (<=256 tokens)? We saw demo numbers but need region-specific baselines.
- How does your model routing handle fallback when a preferred model is out of capacity? Any impact on token costs?
- On hallucination controls: do you provide built-in evals or tooling to measure hallucination rate against our knowledge-base?

We want to run an apples-to-apples evaluation with our internal prompts and a small test set. Can you send a suggested eval plan and any template prompts?

Thanks — Tom
Tom Reynolds
Senior Engineering Manager, DataCloud
From: aditya_rao <aditya@redwood.ai>
To: Tom Reynolds <tom.reynolds@datacloud.io>
Cc: laura_bennett <laura@redwood.ai>, marissa_cole <marissa@redwood.ai>
Date: 2026-02-11T11:03:00-08:00
Subject: Re: Redwood demo — follow-up questions

Tom — great to meet. Quick recap and proposed next steps: 

Recap:
- Latency: our hosted endpoints generally target p50 ~30–60ms for sub-256-token inference in us-west regions on our curated models; hyperscaler-managed GPUs can vary and often have higher cold-start variance.
- Routing/fallbacks: requests are routed by latency/cost policy. If a preferred model is out of capacity we auto-fallback to a compatible variant (same architecture / quantization profile) with graceful degradation. We surface token-cost delta in tracing so you can measure economics.
- Hallucination tooling: Redwood Optimize includes regression testing and hallucination checks tied to prompt sets. We can run token-level trace, F1/precision on extractive tasks, and custom hallucination labeling workflows.

Proposed next tests (to run together):
1) Latency/cost parity: run identical prompt set against Redwood hosted vs your hyperscaler endpoint (same input batch size 1 and 8).
2) Quality/regression: use your sample doc set to evaluate hallucination rate and factual extraction accuracy.
3) Failover/fallback test: simulate preferred-model capacity exhaustion and measure latency/cost impact.

I'll attach a short eval plan and a starter prompt set. Can you share a 200–500 prompt sample (JSONL) and a prioritized list of KPIs (latency p50/p95, hallucination rate tolerance, cost per 1k tokens)?

Next steps:
- Marcus from Product will drop a detailed eval matrix (attachment).
- We can spin up a 1-week dedicated eval instance if you want to avoid noisy shared-hosted results.

Thanks — attaching initial plan.

—Aditya Rao
Account Executive, Redwood Inference
From: marcus_lin <marcus@redwood.ai>
To: aditya_rao <aditya@redwood.ai>, marissa_cole <marissa@redwood.ai>, laura_bennett <laura@redwood.ai>

Date: 2026-02-12T10:45:00-08:00
Subject: Eval plan and metrics (RDW_eval_plan_v1)

Attaching RDW_eval_plan_v1.xlsx — high level notes inline: 

- Tabs: 1) Test matrix (latency/cost/quality), 2) Prompt taxonomy, 3) Hallucination labeling guide, 4) Execution steps.
- Suggested metrics: p50/p95 latency, tokens/sec, cost per 1k tokens, hallucination_rate (false-positive factual assertions per 100 responses), exact-match for extraction tasks, BLEU/ROUGE where applicable.
- Concrete eval prompts: we recommend a mix of: factual QA (KB grounded), instruction transformation, and long-context summarization. 

Execution options:
A) Hosted peer run — fastest, uses your production traffic patterns.
B) Dedicated 1-week eval — most controlled (isolated capacity) and recommended for apples-to-apples.

Marcus Lin
Product Manager, Redwood Inference

Thanks — attached a representative sample (finserv_sample_prompts.jsonl, 320 prompts). Our immediate asks: 

- We care most about hallucination on financial-fact extraction (tickers, transaction amounts) and privacy-sensitive redaction errors.
- Can you run the first pass on your side and return: hallucination_rate for extraction prompts, p50/p95 latency, and a small set of counterexamples where the model hallucinated or invented a source?

Also: any built-in diff tooling to show where your output deviates from hyperscaler outputs? If not, what's your recommended approach?

Sarah Li
Lead ML Engineer, FinServ Inc.

Subject: Re: Redwood vs Hyperscaler inference — post-demo follow-up and next tests

Sarah / Tom — thanks for the sample. Confirming plan and deliverables: 

Deliverables (week 1):
- Redwood runs: run finserv_sample_prompts.jsonl against Redwood hosted curated-model (v1.3-q4a) and against a hyperscaler-managed equivalent model you specified.
- Metrics returned: p50/p95 latency, cost per 1k tokens, hallucination_rate (per our labeling guide), exact-match on extraction tasks, and up to 10 counterexample responses showing hallucinations with short explanation.
- Diff artifact: we will produce a compact CSV diff (prompt_id, rdw_output, hyperscaler_output, diff_type) and a short HTML view for quick review.

Eval specifics / acceptance criteria:
- Hallucination_rate for extraction must be <3% to consider a primary pass (we'll refine with your team).
- p95 latency should be within +/-20% of the hyperscaler baseline for parity in us-west.

Proposed timeline:
- 48 hours: Redwood runs and initial metrics + top 10 counterexamples.
- Day 5: deeper analysis and proposed mitigations (prompt engineering, quantization profile changes, routing tweaks).

Action items for FinServ: share any must-protect fields for privacy redaction check and confirm the hyperscaler endpoint and model name you want us to use for parity runs.

I'll schedule a 30-min sync end-of-week to walk through the diff and counterexamples.

Best —
